title: Design a typeahead search box
source: Popular question on the TryExponent list (tryexponent.com) and in DesignGurus' pattern-based reading list; rubric is original
prompt: Design the search box that suggests completions as the user types, like a search engine's autocomplete. Suggestions must feel instant.
functional: Return up to 10 suggestions for each prefix the user types
Rank suggestions by popularity of the query
Update suggestions as new popular queries appear
non_functional: Suggestions appear within 100 ms
The service stays up during traffic spikes
A few minutes of delay in new popular queries is acceptable
scale: 5 billion searches per day
About 10 suggestion requests per search as the user types
Top 10 million distinct queries kept for suggestions

components.name: Trie or prefix index
components.why: finds all queries that start with the typed prefix quickly

components.name: Ranking by query frequency
components.why: shows the most useful suggestions first

components.name: Query log pipeline
components.why: collects search data and builds new suggestion data

components.name: Cache for popular prefixes
components.why: short prefixes are requested most, so cache them

pitfalls: Querying the full search database for every keystroke
Ranking by insertion order instead of popularity
No plan for updating the trie as trends change
Not sharding the prefix index across servers as the query set grows

title: Design a web crawler
source: Popular question on the TryExponent list (tryexponent.com); rubric is original
prompt: Design a crawler that downloads billions of web pages, extracts their links, and stores the content for a search index without fetching the same page twice.
functional: Start from seed URLs and follow links
Skip pages already crawled or recently crawled
Respect each site's robots.txt and crawl rate
non_functional: The crawler survives a machine failure without losing its progress
Crawling is polite: no more than one request per second per host
Crawled content is stored for later indexing
scale: 10 billion pages
Crawl about 1 billion pages per month
Average page is 500 KB

components.name: URL frontier or queue
components.why: holds URLs waiting to be fetched and orders them by priority and politeness

components.name: Duplicate check store
components.why: avoids fetching the same URL or content twice

components.name: Fetcher workers
components.why: download pages in parallel

components.name: Content storage
components.why: stores 5 PB of page content for the indexer

components.name: robots.txt and politeness cache
components.why: keeps the crawler within each site's rules

pitfalls: Visited set kept in one machine's memory, which does not scale to 10 billion URLs
No politeness rules, so one site gets overloaded
Infinite crawler traps (calendar pages, session IDs) not handled
Storage estimate ignores 500 KB pages at 1 billion per month

title: Design a social media news feed
source: Popular question on the TryExponent list (Instagram and news feed) and on LinkedIn lists of common interview questions; rubric is original
prompt: Design the home feed of a photo-sharing social network. Each user sees recent posts from the people they follow, ranked and loaded quickly.
functional: Users post photos with captions
Home feed shows posts from followed accounts
Feed is ranked and loads 20 posts at a time with infinite scroll
non_functional: Feed loads within 300 ms
New posts appear in followers' feeds within a few seconds
The service stays available during celebrity posts
scale: 500 million daily active users
100 million photos uploaded per day
Average user follows 200 accounts; some accounts have 100 million followers

components.name: Post service
components.why: accepts and stores new posts

components.name: Feed generation or fan-out
components.why: builds each user's feed; the fan-out choice for celebrities is the key trade-off

components.name: Object storage for photos
components.why: stores photos and serves them through a CDN

components.name: Feed cache
components.why: keeps precomputed feeds ready for fast loads

components.name: Follow graph store
components.why: knows who follows whom

pitfalls: Computing the feed on every load by querying all followed accounts
Pushing celebrity posts to 100 million feeds at once with no alternative
Storing photos in the database instead of object storage
No ranking, so the feed is only in time order without any mention of it

title: Design a video streaming platform like YouTube
source: Popular question on the TryExponent list (YouTube, TikTok, Prime Video) and in the Reddit r/leetcode system design breakdowns; rubric is original
prompt: Design a platform where users upload videos and millions of viewers stream them smoothly on phones and TVs at different quality levels.
functional: Upload a video and process it into several resolutions
Stream videos with adaptive quality
Search and view counts
non_functional: Playback starts within 2 seconds
Uploads are never lost
The platform stays up during a major live event
scale: 500 hours of video uploaded per minute
1 billion hours of video watched per day
Average video is 10 minutes, stored in 5 resolutions

components.name: Upload and object storage
components.why: stores the raw uploads durably

components.name: Transcoding pipeline
components.why: turns each upload into several resolutions in the background

components.name: CDN
components.why: serves most video bytes close to the viewer

components.name: Metadata database
components.why: stores titles, owners, and view counts

components.name: Adaptive streaming protocol
components.why: switches quality as bandwidth changes

pitfalls: Serving video from the origin server with no CDN
Transcoding synchronously inside the upload request
Using one resolution for all devices
Counting views with a synchronous database write on every play

title: Design a ride-hailing app like Uber
source: Popular question on the TryExponent list (Design Uber) and in IGotAnOffer's list of common questions; rubric is original
prompt: Design the part of a ride-hailing app that finds nearby drivers for a rider, matches one, and tracks the trip as the driver moves.
functional: Show nearby available drivers to a rider
Match a rider with one driver and handle timeouts
Track driver location every few seconds during a trip
non_functional: Matching completes within 10 seconds
Driver location is at most a few seconds old
A trip is never assigned to two drivers
scale: 5 million drivers sending location every 4 seconds
20 million trips per day
Peak of 3 times the average in busy cities

components.name: Location index
components.why: finds drivers near a point without scanning all drivers

components.name: Location update ingestion
components.why: takes 1.25 million location updates per second

components.name: Matching service
components.why: picks a driver and prevents double assignment

components.name: Trip store
components.why: keeps the trip state and history

pitfalls: Querying the database for drivers within a radius on every request with no spatial index
Storing every location update in the main trip database
No lock or state change when assigning a driver, so two riders get the same driver
Ignoring the peak load in busy cities

title: Design a parking garage reservation and payment system
source: Popular question on the TryExponent list (parking garage reservation and payment); rubric is original
prompt: Design a system that lets drivers reserve a parking spot in a garage, pay for it, and get in and out with a code. Two drivers must never get the same spot for the same time.
functional: Reserve a spot for a time window
Pay by card and get a receipt
Open the gate with a code and check the exit
non_functional: No double booking of a spot
Payment is charged exactly once even if the request is retried
Gate entry works when the internet is down (cached codes)
scale: 200 garages with 500 spots each
100,000 reservations per day
Peak of 5,000 entries in the morning hour

components.name: Reservation service with locking
components.why: prevents two drivers booking the same spot for the same time

components.name: Payment service with idempotency
components.why: charges once, even on retries

components.name: Spot availability store
components.why: holds which spots are free for which times

components.name: Gate controller and offline codes
components.why: lets the gate open without a live connection

pitfalls: Checking availability then booking in two steps with no lock, which allows double booking
Retrying a payment without an idempotency key, which charges twice
Gate depending on the cloud for every entry
No handling for a driver who never leaves or overstays

title: Design live comments for a streaming chat like Twitch
source: Popular question in DesignGurus' pattern-based reading list (live comment streaming like Twitch chat); rubric is original
prompt: Design the live chat beside a stream. A million viewers can read, and a few thousand can post. New messages should appear within about a second.
functional: Viewers see new comments as they arrive
Viewers can post comments with rate limits
Moderators can delete comments
non_functional: Comments appear within 1 second for most viewers
Chat survives a spike when a big event starts
Deleted comments disappear for everyone
scale: 1 million concurrent viewers on one popular stream
5,000 active chatters, sending 20 messages each per minute at peak
Chat history kept for 24 hours

components.name: Fan-out pub/sub or broadcast layer
components.why: delivers each comment to a million viewers without one server doing all the work

components.name: Real-time connection gateway
components.why: keeps viewers connected for live updates

components.name: Rate limiter and moderation
components.why: stops spam and handles deletions

components.name: Recent comment store
components.why: lets a new viewer see recent chat

pitfalls: One server sending each comment to a million connections directly
Polling for new comments every second from a million clients
No rate limit, so a few users flood the chat
Deletions not sent to viewers who already received the comment

title: Design a distributed notification system
source: Popular question on the LinkedIn list of common system design questions (distributed notification system); rubric is original
prompt: Design a service that sends push, email and SMS notifications to users. Other teams call one API to send them, and no notification should be lost or sent twice.
functional: Accept notification requests from other services
Send by push, email, or SMS, respecting each user's preferences
Retry failed sends and report delivery status
non_functional: Urgent notifications (such as OTP codes) go out within 5 seconds
No notification is lost
Duplicate requests from callers do not send twice
scale: 100 million notifications per day, with peaks of 10 times the average
Three channels: push, email, SMS
Users can set quiet hours and opt out per channel

components.name: Notification API and idempotency
components.why: one entry point that drops duplicate requests

components.name: Priority queues per channel
components.why: keeps OTP messages from waiting behind marketing emails

components.name: Channel workers with retries
components.why: send through providers and retry failures

components.name: Preference store
components.why: checks opt-outs and quiet hours before sending

components.name: Delivery status store
components.why: records what was sent and what failed

pitfalls: One shared queue for OTP codes and marketing, so urgent messages wait
No idempotency key, so retries send duplicates
Sending SMS synchronously inside the caller's request
No dead-letter queue, so failed messages disappear

title: Design a metrics and logging service
source: Popular question on the TryExponent list (design a metrics and logging service) and in DesignGurus' reading list on observability; rubric is original
prompt: Design a service that collects metrics and logs from thousands of servers, stores them, and lets engineers query dashboards and set alerts.
functional: Collect metrics and logs from agents on each server
Query a time range and draw a dashboard
Fire an alert when a metric crosses a threshold
non_functional: Data is visible within 30 seconds of being sent
Alerts fire within 1 minute
No data loss during a network partition
scale: 100,000 servers, each sending 1,000 metric points per minute
Logs of 2 TB per day
Metrics kept at full detail for 30 days and downsampled for a year

components.name: Ingestion pipeline with buffering
components.why: absorbs 1.6 million points per second without losing data

components.name: Time-series database
components.why: stores and queries metrics by time efficiently

components.name: Log storage and search
components.why: stores logs cheaply and makes them searchable

components.name: Alerting service
components.why: evaluates rules and notifies on-call

components.name: Downsampling or retention job
components.why: keeps a year of history without full cost

pitfalls: Writing every point synchronously to one database with no buffer
Storing logs and metrics in the same unindexed table
Keeping full resolution for a year, which costs far too much
Alerts computed from a dashboard query instead of a separate rule evaluator
